Closest GRU-family prior art: [Hidasi et al., 2016](https://mquad.github.io/static/papers/2016-feature-rnn-paper.pdf), feature-rich session recommendation combining item IDs and text through GRU architectures; text represented by sparse unigram/bigram features. Establishes precedent for recurrent recommendation with lexical content, but does not establish the exact randomly initialized word-embedding → mean-pooling → ID residual design. [TedRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.18166) studies text–ID fusion and argues that directly adding their embeddings can be ineffective because the representations have different characteristics. No exact match covering the proposed architecture and all requested controls surfaced in this search.

Evidence that text helps is conditional. [TASTE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.14029) reports improved accuracy with reduced popularity bias; [Recformer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13731) reports low-resource and cold-start benefits. These results concern substantially different language-model approaches and do not demonstrate that jointly learned, randomly initialized pooled words provide equivalent gains. Neither result alone separates semantic transfer from lexical identification or popularity correlations.

Recommended controls, rather than established findings: parameter-matched ID-only GRU; fixed item-text permutation retrained from scratch, preferably within training-frequency buckets; random token assignments preserving text lengths and token frequencies; title-only versus description-only variants. Report validation HR@10 by target training frequency, plus lexical-overlap strata. Mean pooling is invariant to word order, so within-item word shuffling is uninformative. Gains over capacity controls and shuffled-text controls, especially for sparse targets and low-overlap histories, would support useful cross-item lexical sharing; they would still fall short of proving semantic understanding. Keep each ablation a single jointly trained GRU model.
